On (salary,dept) the range >80k spans all departments, checking dept per entry. Alphabetical or order-free thinking wastes the seek. Rule: = columns left, one range right, sort/order tail last.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Names never determine seek efficiency.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Leading with the range fans out across every equality value.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Column order decides which seeks are contiguous.

medium.prompt: An index-only scan is possible when…

choices.label: A
choices.body: The table has no primary key defined.

choices.label: B
choices.body: All required columns appear in the index (including INCLUDE/covering columns) so heap access is unnecessary.

choices.label: C
choices.body: The isolation level is READ UNCOMMITTED only.

choices.label: D
choices.body: The query calls arbitrary functions on heap-only columns.

medium.hint: Next step: check the SELECT list against the index payload — any missing column forces heap fetches.
medium.explanation: Visibility plus column coverage lets leaves answer alone.
medium.deepDive: Worked example: SELECT id, email FROM U WHERE dept='Eng' via (dept) INCLUDE (email) never touches the heap (visibility map permitting). Computing lower(heap_only_col) forces heap fetches for that column. PK presence and isolation affect visibility mechanics, not the column-coverage requirement. Coverage first, visibility second.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Primary keys are unrelated to index-only feasibility.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Isolation affects visibility, but covering columns are the main requirement.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Heap-column expressions force heap fetches unless indexed.

medium.prompt: EXPLAIN (or EXPLAIN ANALYZE) shows…

choices.label: A
choices.body: The complete history of every committed transaction.

choices.label: B
choices.body: The ER diagram rendered as SVG.

choices.label: C
choices.body: A list of all user passwords in hashed form.

choices.label: D
choices.body: The optimizer's chosen plan operators and estimated costs (and actual timings with ANALYZE).

medium.hint: Next step: find the highest-cost node — that operator is the tuning target.
medium.explanation: Plan output reveals joins, scans, index usage, and cost estimates for tuning.
medium.deepDive: Worked example: Seq Scan on emp cost=... rows=900k vs Index Scan rows=3 tells you the predicate was not selective enough in the estimate or the index is missing; ANALYZE adds actual ms per node to confirm. Logs, credential catalogs, and ER art live elsewhere. Read EXPLAIN before adding indexes blindly.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Transaction logs are separate audit/recovery artifacts.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: EXPLAIN is execution-plan text, not modeling diagrams.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Security catalogs are not EXPLAIN output.

medium.prompt: A sequential scan is the right choice when…

choices.label: A
choices.body: The query needs exactly one row via a selective key.

choices.label: B
choices.body: The query needs a large fraction of rows or the table is tiny, making index probes wasteful.

choices.label: C
choices.body: The result must be sorted by the primary key.

choices.label: D
choices.body: An index always exists on the filter column.

medium.hint: Next step: compare fraction-needed against the tipping point — large means scan.
medium.explanation: Sweeps beat scattered probes past the selectivity tipping point.
medium.deepDive: Worked example: reading 95% of a 10M-row fact table streams the heap once with prefetch; the indexed path pays 9.5M random fetches. One-row key lookups are the index showcase; index existence alone never mandates use; ordering needs ORDER BY or an ordered path. 'Seq scan' in EXPLAIN is not an insult — it is often optimal.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Single selective rows are the index's best case.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Ordering is guaranteed only by ORDER BY.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Existence does not imply usefulness; the planner weighs costs.

medium.prompt: A hash join typically builds a hash table on…

choices.label: A
choices.body: The transaction log to ensure durability.

choices.label: B
choices.body: The smaller (build) input, probing with the larger (probe) input.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Only columns with UNIQUE constraints disabled.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Always the alphabetically first table name.

medium.hint: Next step: compare input sizes — the smaller side builds.
medium.explanation: Build small, probe large: partition by join key, then match.
medium.deepDive: Worked example: 10k departments build the table; 10M employees stream as probes — memory holds the small side, spilling partitions if needed. Alphabetical names never decide; uniqueness tunes cost, not roles; logs are recovery, not join memory. Equi-joins on big unsorted inputs are hash territory.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Logs are recovery structures, not join hash tables.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Uniqueness affects plan cost but not the build/probe roles directly.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Optimizers pick build side by size/cardinality, not name.

medium.prompt: A sort-merge join is attractive when…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Both inputs are already sorted on the join key (or sorting them is cheaper than hashing).

choices.label: B
choices.body: Both inputs are tiny single-row tables.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Memory is too small to sort anything.

choices.label: D
choices.body: No equality predicate exists at all.

medium.hint: Next step: check input order — sorted on the key means merge is competitive.
medium.explanation: Merge walks two ordered streams in lockstep without a hash table.
medium.deepDive: Worked example: PK-ordered scans of A(id) and B(id) merge in one linear pass — no build memory, sorted output free for ORDER BY id. Tiny tables favor nested loops; non-equi predicates defeat the merge walk; insufficient memory argues for indexed nested loops instead. Sortedness (via indexes or explicit sorts) is the precondition.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Tiny inputs favor nested loops, not merge setup.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Starved memory undermines the sort phase merge needs.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Merge joins need equality to advance both cursors together.

medium.prompt: Why must ANALYZE (statistics update) run after bulk loads?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Because bulk loads delete all indexes automatically.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Because queries are forbidden until ANALYZE commits.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Because row counts and distributions changed, so old cost estimates mislead plan choice.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Because WAL is disabled during loads.

medium.hint: Next step: check last_analyze vs last load — loads newer than stats mean re-analyze.
medium.explanation: Fresh stats keep the cost model honest after data shape shifts.
medium.deepDive: Worked example: table grows 1k→10M rows with stale '1k' stats: planner picks nested loops and a tiny memory budget, then spills and crawls. ANALYZE records 10M rows plus histograms → hash join with proper memory. Loads do not drop indexes; queries still run (poorly); WAL stays on. Stale-stats plans are the first suspect after ETL.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Loads do not drop indexes.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Queries run regardless; plans are just mispriced.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: WAL behavior is independent of statistics.

medium.prompt: Why are indexes created on database columns?

choices.label: A
choices.body: To replace the need for a primary key.

choices.label: B
choices.body: To enforce that no two transactions run concurrently.

choices.label: C
choices.body: To guarantee that every query returns sorted results.

choices.label: D
choices.body: To speed up data retrieval at the cost of extra storage and write overhead.

medium.hint: Next step: weigh read selectivity against write rate — selective reads justify the maintenance tax.
medium.explanation: Indexes are auxiliary access paths (often B-trees) trading writes and space for reads.
medium.deepDive: Worked example: email index turns login lookup from 1M-row scan to 3-level seek, but each user INSERT now writes the heap plus the index, and the structure consumes disk. ORDER BY still governs output order; PKs still enforce identity; concurrency still needs locking. Selective-read workloads win; write-heavy ones feel the tax.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Primary keys enforce uniqueness; indexes are optional helpers.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Concurrency is controlled by locking and isolation, not indexes.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: ORDER BY controls sort order; indexes only help if the planner uses them.

medium.prompt: When does adding an index hurt overall performance?

choices.label: A
choices.body: On read-heavy tables with selective lookups.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Indexes never hurt performance in any workload.

choices.label: C
choices.body: On write-heavy tables where maintenance per INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE outweighs rare read gains.

choices.label: D
choices.body: When the index is never maintained.

medium.hint: Next step: audit index usage stats — unqueried indexes on hot-write tables are drop candidates.
medium.explanation: Every index taxes writes; reads must pay back the cost.
medium.deepDive: Worked example: logging 100k events/sec with 6 secondary indexes spends most I/O maintaining trees nobody queries, halving ingest. The same index on a user table serving 1M selective logins/day pays back hugely. Engines always maintain indexes per write; 'never hurts' ignores this ledger. Index for the reads you have, not the reads you imagine.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Selective reads are the profitable case for indexes.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Write amplification is the standard counterexample.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Maintenance on every write is mandatory, never optional.

hard.prompt: A diagram shows boxes 'Checkout → Validate → Ship' with arrows in time order. Why is this NOT an ER diagram?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Because it lacks SQL code, which every ER diagram must embed.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Because it has only three nodes, while ER diagrams need at least four entities.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Because it models ordered processing steps, while ER models entities, attributes, and relationships without time order.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Because it uses boxes instead of cylinders, which all database diagrams require.

hard.hint: Next step: rewrite each box as a noun and each arrow as 'relates to' — if time order is essential, it is a flowchart.
hard.explanation: Flowcharts answer 'what happens next'; ER answers 'what exists and how it relates'.
hard.deepDive: Worked example: to convert this to ER you would identify nouns — Order, Payment, Shipment — and their links: an Order has one Payment and one Shipment, with attributes like order_date and tracking_no. The arrows 'first validate, then ship' vanish because ER has no sequencing; process order belongs in a flowchart or state diagram. Same domain, two different questions: data shape versus process flow.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: ER diagrams never embed SQL; they are conceptual and map to tables later.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: ER diagrams can have any number of entities, including two; node count is irrelevant.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Cylinders denote storage in some informal sketches, but no shape rule makes a time-ordered flow into ER.

hard.prompt: A table Enroll(student_id, course_id, grade) uses PRIMARY KEY (student_id, course_id). What does this composite key guarantee?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Each student–course pair appears at most once; neither column alone needs to be unique.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Grade is automatically unique across the table.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Either column alone uniquely identifies a row.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Each student takes at most one course and each course has at most one student.

hard.hint: Next step: test the pair — would two rows with identical student_id AND course_id mean the same enrollment? If yes, the composite is right.
hard.explanation: A composite key enforces uniqueness of the combination with minimal columns.
hard.deepDive: Worked example: rows (7,A1,B) and (7,B2,A) coexist because the pairs differ, while a second (7,A1,C) is rejected as a retake row needing an update instead. Minimality matters: dropping course_id would wrongly force one course per student. Composite keys model multi-column identity exactly where single columns cannot.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Non-key columns like grade carry facts; keys never constrain them to be unique.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: If either column alone were unique the second column would be redundant in the key.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: That describes two one-to-one constraints, far stronger than one pair-level constraint.

hard.prompt: Employee(id PK, manager_id FK → Employee.id) models managers. What does manager_id = NULL mean and allow?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Top-level staff with no manager; the FK permits NULL to represent 'no parent' while still checking non-null values.

choices.label: B
choices.body: A corrupt row that violates the foreign key and must be deleted.

choices.label: C
choices.body: A second primary key shadowing the id column.

choices.label: D
choices.body: An index that replaces the foreign key constraint.

hard.hint: Next step: check the roots — exactly the rows that should have no parent carry NULL in the FK.
hard.explanation: Self-referencing FKs model hierarchies; NULL marks the roots.
hard.deepDive: Worked example: CEO row (1, NULL) passes because FK checks are skipped for NULL, while engineer row (9, 1) passes by matching id 1, and row (8, 77) fails since 77 is absent. A foreign key need not share the column name (manager_id vs id) but must match types. NULL here is meaningful — 'has no manager' — unlike a NULL primary key, which is never allowed.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: NULL FK values are explicitly allowed to model roots; they do not violate the constraint.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: A table has one PK; manager_id is a foreign key, not a second PK.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Indexes speed lookups but never replace constraint enforcement.

hard.prompt: A company merges two legacy user databases whose numeric ids overlap. What key strategy best preserves identity?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Concatenate first and last names into a new natural primary key.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Drop all keys and rely on row order for identity.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Introduce a new surrogate user_id and keep legacy ids as ordinary mapped attributes.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Keep both legacy id schemes as a shared primary key.

hard.hint: Next step: mint one fresh id space, then record each legacy id as data, not identity.
hard.explanation: Merges with colliding domains need a fresh meaningless identifier.
hard.deepDive: Worked example: legacy A user 42 (Ann) and legacy B user 42 (Bo) collide, so neither 42 can remain the PK. New surrogates 1001→(A,42,Ann) and 1002→(B,42,Bo) disambiguate, with legacy_id kept as data for lookup scripts. Child tables point at 1001/1002 uniformly. Names collide too and change on marriage, so they fail stability and uniqueness as keys.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Names are neither unique nor stable, failing both key requirements at once.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Row order shifts on every vacuum/reload; it is never a valid identity mechanism.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Overlapping domains guarantee PK collisions; one PK cannot hold two meanings for 42.

hard.prompt: Given a 1-N relationship Department (1) — Employee (N), where must the foreign key be placed?

choices.label: A
choices.body: In Department as a list of all its employee ids.

choices.label: B
choices.body: In Employee as dept_id referencing Department, because each N-side row points at its single parent.

choices.label: C
choices.body: In a junction table, as with many-to-many.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Nowhere; 1-N relationships need no foreign key.

hard.hint: Next step: find the 'many' side — the FK column goes there, one value per row.
hard.explanation: The FK sits on the many side pointing at the one side.
hard.deepDive: Worked example: Employee(Ann, dept 5), (Bo, dept 5), (Cy, dept 9) stores one dept_id per employee — fixed width, joinable, constrainable. Putting emp_ids in Department needs a variable-length set violating 1NF, and a junction table adds pointless rows for a shape one FK already captures. Read cardinality, then place the key: many side holds it.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Multi-valued columns violate atomicity and cannot be foreign keys.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Junction tables are for M-N; using one for 1-N adds redundant joins.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Without a FK the database cannot enforce or join the assignment.

hard.prompt: For junction Enrollment(student_id FK, course_id FK, grade), what is the natural primary key and why?

choices.label: A
choices.body: The composite (student_id, course_id), since each pairing occurs at most once and identifies the grade.

choices.label: B
choices.body: grade alone, since grades identify rows.

choices.label: C
choices.body: student_id alone, since students are unique.

choices.label: D
choices.body: course_id alone, since courses are unique.

hard.hint: Next step: test duplicates — should the same student–course pair appear twice? If no, key the pair.
hard.explanation: The junction PK is the pair of FKs; it bans duplicate enrollment.
hard.deepDive: Worked example: (7,A1,B) and (7,B2,A) coexist, but a second (7,A1,C) is rejected — a retake must UPDATE the grade, not duplicate the pairing. student_id alone would limit each student to one course; course_id alone to one student. Grade is a fact, not an identity, and duplicates freely across rows.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Non-key facts like grades repeat constantly and can never identify rows.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: One side's id alone enforces one-to-many, destroying the many-to-many shape.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: The mirror image: one course, one student — not an enrollment system.

hard.prompt: Which mechanism is the declarative way to guarantee 'every order references a real customer'?

choices.label: A
choices.body: A trigger-free application check performed once a month.

choices.label: B
choices.body: A longer VARCHAR width on the customer name column.

choices.label: C
choices.body: An index on Orders.customer_id alone.

choices.label: D
choices.body: A foreign-key constraint from Orders.customer_id to Customer.id.

hard.hint: Next step: ask 'which writes must the database itself reject?' — that answer is always a constraint.
hard.explanation: Referential rules belong in FK constraints, not in indexes or app code.
hard.deepDive: Worked example: with the FK declared, Order(customer 404-ghost) fails at INSERT time in every session, including ad-hoc psql, while an index alone would store the ghost id faster without complaint. Monthly app checks leave weeks of bad data. Column width limits string length, never cross-table existence. Declare the invariant once; the engine enforces it on all paths.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Periodic checks permit violations between runs; constraints permit none.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Widths police string length, not whether a parent row exists.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Indexes accelerate lookups; they accept any value including dangling ids.

hard.prompt: What is an identifying relationship in ER modeling?

choices.label: A
choices.body: A relationship that deletes all indexes when used.

choices.label: B
choices.body: A relationship whose parent key migrates into the child's primary key, used for weak entities.

choices.label: C
choices.body: A relationship between two databases on different servers.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Any relationship drawn with a thicker line for emphasis.

hard.hint: Next step: inspect the child PK — if it contains the parent's key, the relationship is identifying.
hard.explanation: Identifying = parent key becomes part of child PK.
hard.deepDive: Worked example: Building(1) —< Room(1,101),(1,102): the relationship 'contains' contributes building_id into Room's PK (building_id, room_no). Non-identifying links like Employee.dept_id stay outside the child's PK. The cascade often follows: remove building 1 and its identified rooms vanish. Line thickness is notation, not semantics.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Relationships never drop indexes; storage choices are independent.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: ER relationships are intra-schema; cross-server links are federation concerns.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Notation weight carries no semantics; key migration does.

hard.prompt: Subtypes FullTime and PartTime share most Employee attributes but each adds a few. Which mapping preserves constraints most precisely, at the cost of joins?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Storing subtype rows as JSON files outside the database.

choices.label: B
choices.body: One table per subtype sharing the PK (joined-subtype tables with FK to Employee).

choices.label: C
choices.body: Stuffing every subtype attribute into one wide table with many NULLs.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Deleting the shared attributes entirely.

hard.hint: Next step: list each subtype's mandatory columns — if they differ, separate tables enforce them exactly.
hard.explanation: Joined subtype tables enforce per-subtype NOT NULLs cleanly but require joins to reassemble.
hard.deepDive: Worked example: Employee(id,name) plus FullTime(id FK PK, salary) with salary NOT NULL and PartTime(id FK PK, hourly_rate) with hourly_rate NOT NULL — each subtype's rule holds exactly. Single-table inheritance forces salary/hourly_rate nullable with CHECKs to fake exclusivity. Precise constraints cost a join per read; the wide table saves joins but weakens guarantees.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: External files abandon constraints, joins, and transactions entirely.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Wide tables trade precision for read speed, leaving subtype rules to CHECKs and NULLs.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Shared attributes are the point of the supertype; deleting them destroys the model.

hard.prompt: Why is SELECT * FROM T WHERE a NOT IN (1, 2, NULL) risky when the list contains NULL?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Because NOT IN with NULL returns every row twice.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Because any comparison against the NULL makes the predicate unknown, so NOT IN returns no rows.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Because the query deletes the NULL row.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Because NOT IN ignores all non-null list values.

hard.hint: Next step: check the subquery column for NULLs — if any exist, rewrite with NOT EXISTS.
hard.explanation: NOT IN with a NULL in the set filters out everything; prefer NOT EXISTS.
hard.deepDive: Worked example: row a=5 checks 5<>1 (true) AND 5<>2 (true) AND 5<>NULL (unknown) → overall unknown → discarded. Every candidate row meets the same fate, so the result is empty regardless of data. Rewrite as WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM U WHERE U.x = T.a), which handles NULLs correctly. This NULL-poisoning trap is why linters flag NOT IN on nullable columns.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Nothing is duplicated; the failure mode is zero rows, not doubled rows.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: SELECT never deletes; the symptom is an empty result set.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Non-null values are still compared; the NULL poisons the AND chain to unknown.

hard.prompt: Why can SELECT COUNT(*) FROM A JOIN B ON A.x = NULL never return correct matches?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Because the tables must first be denormalized.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Because joins forbid NULL columns entirely.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Because A.x = NULL is always unknown, so the join predicate is never true.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Because COUNT(*) skips NULL rows automatically.

hard.hint: Next step: rewrite the predicate with IS NULL tests for the missing-value case.
hard.explanation: Join predicates need true; comparisons with NULL yield unknown and match nothing.
hard.deepDive: Worked example: every candidate pair evaluates x = NULL → unknown, and ON keeps only true pairs, so the join is empty even when 'matching' NULLs face each other. To match missing values explicitly, write ON (A.x = B.x OR (A.x IS NULL AND B.x IS NULL)). NULLs join like they compare: never equal under =.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Schema shape is irrelevant; three-valued logic blocks the predicate.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Nullable columns join fine on their known values; only NULL-to-anything never matches.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: COUNT(*) counts all joined rows including NULLs; filtering happens in ON, not COUNT.

hard.prompt: SELECT COUNT(*) vs COUNT(email) on a table where some emails are NULL differ how?

choices.label: A
choices.body: They always return identical values.

choices.label: B
choices.body: COUNT(*) counts all rows; COUNT(email) skips rows where email is NULL.

choices.label: C
choices.body: COUNT(email) counts NULLs while COUNT(*) skips them.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Both skip NULL rows entirely.

hard.hint: Next step: ask 'should missing values count?' — yes means COUNT(*), no means COUNT(col).
hard.explanation: COUNT(*) counts rows; COUNT(col) counts known values in that column.
hard.deepDive: Worked example: rows {(1,'a'),(2,NULL),(3,'b')} give COUNT(*)=3 but COUNT(email)=2 — the NULL row vanishes from the second tally. COUNT(DISTINCT email) would further dedupe to 2 here (a,b). Choosing wrongly undercounts rosters or overcounts contacts; match the function to 'rows' versus 'known values'.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: NULL-skipping makes them differ exactly when NULLs exist.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: The skipping is reversed: column counts skip NULLs, row counts do not.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: COUNT(*) never skips; it tallies every row in the group.

hard.prompt: Why does NULLIF(a, b) exist given CASE expressions?

choices.label: A
choices.body: It deletes rows where a equals b.

choices.label: B
choices.body: It creates an index on the two columns.

choices.label: C
choices.body: It concisely returns NULL when a equals b, avoiding divide-by-zero and sentinel values.

choices.label: D
choices.body: It replaces all NULLs in a column with b permanently.

hard.hint: Next step: spot the 'special value meaning missing' — wrap it in NULLIF to restore real NULLs.
hard.explanation: NULLIF(a,b) is shorthand for CASE WHEN a=b THEN NULL ELSE a END.
hard.deepDive: Worked example: SUM(x) / NULLIF(COUNT(y), 0) yields NULL instead of a division error when no y rows exist. Sentinel tricks like storing -1 for missing pollute MIN/AVG, while NULLIF converts the sentinel back to missing at query time: NULLIF(code, -1). It transforms values per row; it never updates, deletes, or indexes anything.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: SELECT expressions never delete rows.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Indexing is DDL; NULLIF is a scalar function.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: NULLIF is a per-row expression, not an UPDATE; stored data is untouched.

hard.prompt: A scalar subquery in the SELECT list must satisfy what requirement?

choices.label: A
choices.body: It must run at SERIALIZABLE isolation.

choices.label: B
choices.body: It must return at most one row and one column per outer row, else the query errors.

choices.label: C
choices.body: It must return the entire table contents.

choices.label: D
choices.body: It must modify the rows it reads.

hard.hint: Next step: run the subquery for one outer row — more than one value means wrong construct.
hard.explanation: Scalar position demands a single value per row.
hard.deepDive: Worked example: SELECT name, (SELECT AVG(s) FROM Emp e2 WHERE e2.dept=e1.dept) FROM Emp e1 yields each employee beside their dept average — one number per row. If the subquery returned two rows, the engine cannot fit them into one cell and raises 'more than one row returned'. Multi-row needs IN/EXISTS/JOIN instead. Shape errors are the telltale scalar-subquery bug.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Isolation is independent of subquery shape requirements.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Whole-table output belongs in FROM/JOIN, never in a scalar slot.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: SELECT subqueries are read-only; writes need INSERT/UPDATE.

hard.prompt: Why is LIMIT 10 without ORDER BY unreliable for 'top 10' reports?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Because without ORDER BY the engine may return any 10 rows in any order, varying run to run.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Because the query will always return zero rows.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Because LIMIT requires GROUP BY to function.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Because LIMIT locks the table first.

hard.hint: Next step: add ORDER BY with a unique tiebreaker before trusting any LIMIT cut.
hard.explanation: No ORDER BY means no defined order — 'first 10' is meaningless.
hard.deepDive: Worked example: two runs of SELECT * FROM Emp LIMIT 2 can return (Ann,Bo) then (Cy,Ann) after a vacuum or parallel scan reshuffles heap order. Adding ORDER BY salary DESC fixes the set deterministically (plus a tiebreaker id for equal salaries). Reports and pagination must always pair LIMIT with ORDER BY.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Nonempty tables return rows; the problem is which rows, not zero.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: LIMIT works standalone; determinism is what requires ORDER BY.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: LIMIT takes no locks beyond normalMVCC reads.

hard.prompt: A SQL view is…

choices.label: A
choices.body: A stored query definition that behaves like a virtual table.

choices.label: B
choices.body: An index organized by column cardinality.

choices.label: C
choices.body: A physical copy of data refreshed only on restart.

choices.label: D
choices.body: A transaction isolation level.

hard.hint: Next step: check storage — if no rows are stored, it is an ordinary virtual view.
hard.explanation: Views encapsulate queries; most are virtual, some materialized.
hard.deepDive: Worked example: CREATE VIEW Big(E) AS SELECT * FROM Emp WHERE salary>100k lets SELECT * FROM Big(E) reuse the filter; base-table writes appear immediately since nothing is stored. A materialized view instead stores rows and needs REFRESH to catch up. Some simple views accept INSERT/UPDATE under strict rules; isolation levels and indexes are unrelated concepts.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Indexes are storage structures, not named queries.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: That describes a materialized view, which stores results physically.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Isolation levels are transaction properties, not query definitions.

hard.prompt: RANK() versus DENSE_RANK() over ORDER BY score DESC differ how on tied scores {100, 100, 90}?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Both give {1, 2, 3} ignoring ties.

choices.label: B
choices.body: RANK gives random numbers while DENSE_RANK sorts.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Both delete the tied rows.

choices.label: D
choices.body: RANK gives {1, 1, 3} skipping 2; DENSE_RANK gives {1, 1, 2} without a gap.

hard.hint: Next step: write positions with ties shared, then check whether the next number skips.
hard.explanation: RANK leaves gaps after ties; DENSE_RANK compacts them.
hard.deepDive: Worked example: Ann and Bo tie at 100 (both rank 1); Cy at 90 is third competitor (RANK 3) but second distinct score (DENSE 2). ROW_NUMBER would force {1,2,3} distinct. Leaderboards use RANK for '3rd person' semantics and DENSE for '2nd distinct score' semantics. The gap is the entire difference.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Forcing distinct numbers is ROW_NUMBER, not either RANK variant.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Both are deterministic given ORDER BY; randomness never appears.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Ranking never deletes; all three rows remain with their ranks.

hard.prompt: How do you compute a running total of daily sales with a window function?

choices.label: A
choices.body: COUNT(*) with PARTITION BY day only.

choices.label: B
choices.body: SUM(amount) OVER (ORDER BY day ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING)

choices.label: C
choices.body: GROUP BY day with no window clause.

choices.label: D
choices.body: ORDER BY day alone with no aggregate.

hard.hint: Next step: add the frame 'from first row to current row' after ORDER BY day.
hard.explanation: A cumulative frame sums all rows from the start through the current day.
hard.deepDive: Worked example: amounts {10, 20, 30} on days 1–3 yield running {10, 30, 60}: each row sums its frame (start→current). Omitting the frame defaults vary by engine, so state ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING explicitly. GROUP BY gives per-day {10,20,30} without accumulation; bare ORDER BY sorts only. Frame clauses control the accumulation window.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Per-day counts give 1 each, never a cumulative sum.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: GROUP BY collapses to daily subtotals without carrying history forward.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Sorting alone computes nothing; an aggregate plus frame is required.

hard.prompt: What is the closure of {A} given FDs A → B, B → C, C → D?

choices.label: A
choices.body: {A, B} only, because chains longer than one step are forbidden.

choices.label: B
choices.body: {A} alone, because closures never expand.

choices.label: C
choices.body: {D} only, because closure returns just the final attribute.

choices.label: D
choices.body: {A, B, C, D}, by repeatedly applying each FD until nothing new appears.

hard.hint: Next step: loop — after each addition, re-check every FD for a newly satisfied left side.
hard.explanation: Closure accumulates every attribute reachable through the FD graph.
hard.deepDive: Worked example: start {A}; A→B adds B; now B present so B→C adds C; now C present so C→D adds D — fixpoint {A,B,C,D}. Each pass re-scans all FDs with the enlarged set. Since closure(A) covers everything, A is a key, and A→D is an implied (transitive) FD. The algorithm terminates because attributes are finite.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Transitivity chains compose without length limits; that is the point of closure.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Expansion is the entire purpose of the closure algorithm.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Closure returns the full reachable set, not just the endpoint.

hard.prompt: Decomposing Enroll(sid,cid,sname) into S(sid,sname) + E(sid,cid) to fix 2NF preserves information only if the decomposition is…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Lossless: joining S and E on sid recovers exactly the original rows.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Lossy but dependency-preserving, which is preferred over lossless.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Automatic regardless of the join column.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Lossless only when both tables share no columns.

hard.hint: Next step: join the fragments on the key and diff against the original — any extra or missing row fails.
hard.explanation: 2NF surgery must not invent or lose pairings — the join must reconstruct the source.
hard.deepDive: Worked example: S{(7,Ann)} joined with E{(7,A1),(7,B2)} on sid rebuilds (7,A1,Ann),(7,B2,Ann) exactly. Joining on a non-key like sname instead could cross-multiply Ann rows into spurious (7,B2) duplicates. The chase test formalizes this: the common columns must functionally determine one side. Fix partial dependencies, then verify lossless reconstruction.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Lossy decompositions corrupt data; lossless is mandatory, dependency preservation secondary.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Join column choice decides losslessness; arbitrary splits lose information.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Lossless joins require shared columns — typically a key of one fragment.

hard.prompt: R(Student, Course, Instructor) with (Student,Course) key and Instructor → Course is in 3NF but not BCNF. Why does 3NF tolerate it?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Because Course is prime (part of a candidate key), and 3NF permits non-key determinants of prime attributes.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Because transitive dependencies never matter.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Because Instructor is a foreign key.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Because the relation has only three columns.

hard.hint: Next step: check whether the dependent is prime — prime endpoints pass 3NF but face BCNF scrutiny.
hard.explanation: 3NF's prime-attribute exception is the gap BCNF closes.
hard.deepDive: Worked example: Instructor Smith always teaches DB, so Smith → DB with Smith a non-superkey — BCNF fails since the determinant is not a superkey. But Course belongs to candidate key (Student,Course), i.e., it is prime, so 3NF's rule (endpoints must be prime or the determinant a superkey) passes. Overlapping candidate keys create exactly this wedge. BCNF demands every determinant be a superkey with no prime exception.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Transitives are 3NF's core concern; the prime exception is the subtlety.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Key roles elsewhere do not change determinant analysis here.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Column count never decides normal forms.

hard.prompt: BCNF can be stricter than 3NF when…

choices.label: A
choices.body: The table has no functional dependencies at all.

choices.label: B
choices.body: All attributes are prime (part of some candidate key).

choices.label: C
choices.body: A relation has overlapping candidate keys so a non-superkey determinant of a prime attribute remains.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Every determinant is a single-attribute primary key.

hard.hint: Next step: look for two keys sharing columns — overlap plus a prime dependent means 3NF/BCNF split.
hard.explanation: Overlapping keys open the 3NF prime-exception wedge that BCNF shuts.
hard.deepDive: Worked example: R(Student,Course,Instructor), keys (Student,Course) and (Student,Instructor), FD Instructor → Course: Course is prime so 3NF passes, yet Instructor is no superkey so BCNF fails. Decomposition into (Instructor,Course) + (Student,Instructor) achieves BCNF but may sacrifice the (Student,Course) dependency check. Single-attribute keys and FD-free tables collapse the distinction; all-prime tables still admit the wedge via overlap.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Without FDs, normal forms trivially hold at every level.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: All-prime alone is insufficient; overlap is the wedge mechanism.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Then BCNF and 3NF often coincide with no wedge.

hard.prompt: Decomposing a 3NF relation to BCNF sometimes loses dependency preservation. What does that trade-off mean?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Some FD can no longer be checked within a single table and would need a join to enforce.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Rows are always lost in the process.

choices.label: C
choices.body: BCNF tables can never be joined back together.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Indexes are destroyed permanently.

hard.hint: Next step: locate each FD's columns after the split — an FD spanning fragments is no longer locally checkable.
hard.explanation: BCNF-first versus dependency-preservation-first is a genuine design tension.
hard.deepDive: Worked example: splitting R(S,C,I) to fix Instructor → Course yields fragments where the (Student,Course) pairing constraint spans tables — inserts need a cross-table join check or an application trigger instead of a cheap intra-row UNIQUE. Some shops stay in 3NF deliberately to keep that check local. Lossless join still holds (no rows lost); what degrades is enforcement locality, not recoverability.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Lossless decomposition loses no rows; enforcement locality is what degrades.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: BCNF fragments join back losslessly by design.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Indexes are rebuilt freely around any decomposition.

hard.prompt: How does normalization trade read performance against anomalies?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Normal forms affect only storage size, never queries.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Denormalization eliminates all anomalies.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Normalization always speeds every query.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Higher normal forms remove redundancy-driven anomalies but add joins that can slow reads; denormalization reverses the trade.

hard.hint: Next step: map the workload — write-heavy integrity favors normalize, hot analytic scans may denormalize.
hard.explanation: Anomaly-freedom costs joins; read speed costs redundancy.
hard.deepDive: Worked example: normalized Emp ⨝ Dept reassembles (name, building) per query — anomaly-free but join-paying — while EmpWide(id,name,building) reads in one scan yet renames buildings across hundreds of rows. Warehouses denormalize hot paths deliberately, accepting controlled redundancy with batch rebuilds. Neither direction dominates; workload decides.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Join counts and redundancy both shape query cost directly.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Denormalization introduces redundancy, hence more anomaly exposure.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Joins add read cost; normalization optimizes correctness, not speed.

hard.prompt: When is a BCNF decomposition guaranteed lossless?

choices.label: A
choices.body: When the common attributes of the fragments form a superkey of at least one fragment.

choices.label: B
choices.body: When no functional dependencies hold.

choices.label: C
choices.body: When the fragments share no attributes at all.

choices.label: D
choices.body: When both fragments have the same number of rows.

hard.hint: Next step: intersect the fragments — verify the shared set is a key of one side.
hard.explanation: Shared-key condition is the lossless-join test for binary splits.
hard.deepDive: Worked example: R(A,B,C) with A→B splits into R1(A,B)+R2(A,C): common {A} is a key of R1, so rejoining on A rebuilds exactly. Splitting instead into (A,B)+(B,C) on common {B} (not a key of either) fabricates spurious (A,C) combos. Check keyhood of the intersection before splitting; row counts never decide it.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: FD-free splits still need the key condition to avoid cross products.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Disjoint fragments cannot rejoin at all; sharing is required.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Row counts are data accidents, not structural guarantees.

hard.prompt: Why might a designer stop at 3NF instead of pushing every table to BCNF?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Because 3NF tables cannot be joined.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Because 3NF forbids all redundancy while BCNF allows it.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Because some BCNF splits sacrifice dependency preservation, forcing cross-table enforcement.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Because BCNF is weaker than 3NF.

hard.hint: Next step: weigh insert-path checks — if BCNF moves a check across tables, 3NF may be the pragmatic stop.
hard.explanation: Keeping FDs locally checkable can outweigh BCNF purity.
hard.deepDive: Worked example: R(Student,Course,Instructor) in 3NF keeps its pairing constraint checkable in one row; the BCNF split scatters it so inserts need join-validated triggers. Shops with heavy write integrity keep 3NF and document the residual redundancy. BCNF is strictly stronger on redundancy, and 3NF tables join normally — the cost is enforcement locality, not capability.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: 3NF relations join like any others.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: BCNF removes more redundancy than 3NF, not less.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: BCNF implies 3NF; it is the stronger form.

hard.prompt: Fifth normal form (5NF / PJ-NF) deals with…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Mandatory clustered indexes on foreign keys.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Encrypting attributes at rest.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Only tables with exactly five columns.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Join dependencies that cannot be reconstructed from smaller projections without spurious tuples.

hard.hint: Next step: try pairwise projections and rejoin — phantom rows mean the ternary must stay whole (5NF).
hard.explanation: 5NF splits relations when rejoining fragments invents phantom rows.
hard.deepDive: Worked example: Supply(vendor, part, project) where valid triples are constrained jointly — no FD or multivalued split captures it, yet projecting into three binary tables and rejoining fabricates vendor-part-project combos never supplied. 5NF keeps the ternary table precisely because pairwise fragments lie. Rare in practice, it is the limit case: decompose only when fragments rejoin faithfully.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Physical design is separate from 5NF.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Security is orthogonal to PJ/NF.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: The 'fifth' refers to normal form level, not column count.

hard.prompt: Write skew happens when…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Two transactions read overlapping data, make disjoint writes from stale reads, and together violate an invariant.

choices.label: B
choices.body: The database rejects all SERIALIZABLE transactions.

choices.label: C
choices.body: An index is rebuilt during SELECT.

choices.label: D
choices.body: A single UPDATE touches every row in the table.

hard.hint: Next step: check joint outcome — individually-valid writes that together break a rule mean skew.
hard.explanation: Classic: two on-call doctors each see coverage, both sign off, leaving zero — needs serializable or constraints.
hard.deepDive: Worked example: rule '≥1 doctor on call'; Ann and Bo each read {Ann,Bo} on-call, Ann removes herself, Bo removes himself — each write is locally sensible, jointly violating. Snapshot isolation permits it (disjoint writes, no conflict); SERIALIZABLE aborts one, or a CHECK/count constraint blocks the second commit. Bulk updates are not skew; serializable prevents rather than defines it.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Serializable prevents write skew; it does not define it.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Maintenance operations are unrelated.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Bulk update is not write skew.

hard.prompt: READ UNCOMMITTED differs from READ COMMITTED in that it…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Guarantees full serializability.

choices.label: B
choices.body: May return uncommitted (dirty) data that could later be rolled back.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Hides all concurrent writes including committed ones.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Locks every row it touches exclusively.

hard.hint: Next step: check writer commit state — RU is the only level that exposes the uncommitted value.
hard.explanation: RU is the weakest level: no read locks, dirties possible.
hard.deepDive: Worked example: balance 100→200 uncommitted is readable as 200 under RU (then vanishes on rollback), while RC shows 100 until commit. Engines like Postgres map RU to RC internally; usage is rare outside approximate analytics. Stronger guarantees and locking belong to higher levels, never RU.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Serial equivalence is SERIALIZABLE's promise, RU's opposite.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: RC-grade hiding of uncommitted data is exactly what RU drops.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: RU takes minimal locks; exclusivity is a write concept.

hard.prompt: Under snapshot isolation, first-committer-wins on overlapping writes means…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Two concurrent transactions writing the same row: the first to commit succeeds, the later gets a write-write conflict error.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Reads block until every writer commits.

choices.label: C
choices.body: All writes always succeed regardless of conflicts.

choices.label: D
choices.body: The last reader decides which write survives.

hard.hint: Next step: overlap the write sets — shared rows mean second committer aborts.
hard.explanation: SI detects write-write overlap at commit and aborts the loser.
hard.deepDive: Worked example: T1 and T2 both update seat 5 from snapshot $200 → $250 and $260; T1 commits, T2's commit raises 'conflicting update' and must retry on fresh data. Disjoint writes (different rows) both pass — which is why skew sneaks through. Conflict scope is row-level overlap, reads never decide, and retries are the app's job.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: MVCC readers never block writers.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Overlapping SI writes conflict; only disjoint writes both pass.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Readers do not arbitrate write conflicts.

hard.prompt: Why does snapshot isolation still permit write skew?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Because the two transactions write disjoint rows, so no write-write conflict fires despite stale reads.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Because SI takes no snapshots at all.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Because skew requires a deadlock cycle.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Because SI allows dirty reads of uncommitted data.

hard.hint: Next step: diff the write sets — disjoint writes with a shared read predicate spell skew-prone SI.
hard.explanation: Skew hides in disjoint writes; SI only guards overlapping ones.
hard.deepDive: Worked example: Ann deletes her on-call row, Bo deletes his — different rows, both commits pass, yet joint invariant '≥1 on call' breaks. First-committer-wins sees no overlap to reject. SERIALIZABLE's predicate tracking (SSI) spots the shared read pattern and aborts one. Skew is the price of SI's non-blocking reads; constraints or serializable close it.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Snapshots are SI's foundation, not its absence.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Deadlock cycles are unrelated to skew's disjoint-write shape.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: SI never shows uncommitted data; reads are snapshot-stable.

hard.prompt: Strict 2PL differs from basic 2PL in that it…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Releases exclusive locks immediately after each write.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Skips locking reads entirely.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Commits before acquiring any lock.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Holds all locks (especially exclusive) until commit/abort, preventing cascading rollbacks.

hard.hint: Next step: check unlock timing — X released before end means not strict.
hard.explanation: Strict = no unlock until end; recoverability without cascades.
hard.deepDive: Worked example: T1 writes X uncommitted; under basic 2PL releasing X early lets T2 read the dirty value, so T1's abort forces T2's abort (cascade). Strict holds X to COMMIT — T2 waits, reads only committed data, never cascades. Cost is longer lock holds (less concurrency) for simpler recovery. Rigorous 2PL extends holding to reads too.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Early X release is basic 2PL's cascade-prone behavior.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Read locking discipline is orthogonal to the strict/basic split.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Locks precede commit; commit-then-lock is impossible.

hard.prompt: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE is used to…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Delete the selected rows immediately.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Take exclusive locks on the selected rows to prevent concurrent modification (e.g., lost updates).

choices.label: C
choices.body: Speed up the SELECT by skipping all locks.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Change the isolation level of the session.

hard.hint: Next step: updating rows you just read? Re-read them with FOR UPDATE inside the same transaction.
hard.explanation: Pessimistic lock the exact rows you intend to update.
hard.deepDive: Worked example: booking seat 5: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE locks the row; a rival's identical statement blocks until you COMMIT/ROLLBACK, serializing the sale. Plain SELECT takes no blocking write lock, so both sellers could oversell. Deletion needs DELETE; isolation needs SET TRANSACTION. Lock-then-update in one transaction is the lost-update antidote.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Selection with locks modifies nothing by itself.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: FOR UPDATE adds locks; it never skips them.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Isolation is set explicitly, not by row locking.

hard.prompt: Which practice most effectively reduces deadlock frequency?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Access rows in random order per transaction.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Acquire locks in a consistent global order and keep transactions short with minimal lock footprints.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Hold locks as long as possible across user think-time.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Disable deadlock detection to save overhead.

hard.hint: Next step: sort each transaction's lock targets identically — global order first, shrinking footprint second.
hard.explanation: Ordered, short, narrow locking starves cycles of opportunity.
hard.deepDive: Worked example: all money-movement units lock accounts by ascending id — T1 (3→7) and T2 (7→3) both lock 3 first, so one waits instead of cycling. Holding locks through user input or random orders manufactures crossings. Detection stays on as the safety net; ordering is the prevention. Fewer locks + same order + short units = rare deadlocks.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Random orders manufacture the crossings that cycles need.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Open-ended holds across think-time maximize cycle windows.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Disabling detection turns recoverable aborts into hangs.

hard.prompt: Optimistic concurrency control (OCC) typically…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Validates at commit that no conflicting writes occurred since the snapshot/read set.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Requires denormalized schemas only.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Locks every row on first SELECT FOR UPDATE automatically.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Disallows any read operations.

hard.hint: Next step: version-stamp your read set — changed versions at commit mean abort and retry.
hard.explanation: OCC: read freely, check versions at commit, abort on conflict.
hard.deepDive: Worked example: T1 snapshots seat map, picks seat 5; T2 concurrently books 5 and commits; T1's commit validation sees seat 5's version advanced and aborts — retry shows it taken. Low-conflict workloads skip locking overhead; high-conflict ones thrash with retries. Locking rows eagerly is pessimistic 2PL, reads are OCC's bulk phase, and schemas are orthogonal.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Schema style is independent of OCC.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: That is pessimistic locking, not OCC.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: OCC relies on reads with validation.

hard.prompt: Why must a COMMIT wait for log fsync (group commit aside) before acknowledging?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Becausefsync speeds up future SELECTs directly.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Otherwise a crash could lose acknowledged committed work, breaking durability.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Because locks cannot release without fsync.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Because checksums require acknowledgement first.

hard.hint: Next step: place the crash between ack and disk — any lost acked work means the ordering is wrong.
hard.explanation: Ack means durable: the log proves it on stable storage.
hard.deepDive: Worked example: ack-then-fsync loses charge 101 on power failure a millisecond later — the user was told 'paid' but restart shows nothing. Waiting for fsync (batched across concurrent committers via group commit) bounds this to true media failure. Lock release follows commit; SELECT speed and checksums are separate concerns. No fsync, no promise.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: fsync serves durability; read speed comes from buffers and indexes.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Lock release timing is independent of the durability proof.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Checksums validate pages; they do not gate acknowledgement.

hard.prompt: When does a B-tree point lookup perform worse than a sequential scan?

choices.label: A
choices.body: When the predicate matches exactly one row.

choices.label: B
choices.body: When the table fits in one page.

choices.label: C
choices.body: When the predicate matches a large fraction of rows, turning many random probes costlier than one sweep.

choices.label: D
choices.body: B-trees always beat scans in every case.

hard.hint: Next step: estimate the match fraction — large fractions favor scans.
hard.explanation: Selectivity decides: scattered many-row fetches lose to sequential sweeps.
hard.deepDive: Worked example: status='shipped' on 90% of 10M rows via index means ~9M random row fetches; a sequential scan streams the heap once with prefetch. The optimizer's tipping point (often ~5–10% depending on clustering) switches plans. Single-row lookups are the index's best case; tiny tables are decided by caching. 'Always index' ignores this crossover.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Single-row seeks are the index's strongest case.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Tiny tables are cache-resident either way; the crossover matters at scale.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: High-match-fraction scans are the standard counterexample.

hard.prompt: What is an index skip scan and when does it help?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Ignoring the index and always scanning the heap.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Deleting leading-column values to shrink the index.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Skipping index maintenance on all writes.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Probing each distinct leading-column value to use a composite index when the leading column is unconstrained but low-cardinality.

hard.hint: Next step: count distinct leading values — few means skip scan may win, many means it loses.
hard.explanation: Skip scan trades N mini-seeks (N = distinct leading values) for a full scan.
hard.deepDive: Worked example: index (country, city) with 5 countries, query city='Paris': five seeks (one per country) beat scanning millions. With 5M distinct leading values the probes cost more than the scan and the planner declines. Maintenance still happens per write; heap scans are the alternative, not the technique. Low-cardinality gaps enable it; high-cardinality gaps defeat it.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Skip scan uses the index creatively; it never ignores it.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Values are never deleted to enable plans.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Maintenance continues on every write regardless.

hard.prompt: A partial index (filtered index) indexes…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Only rows that violate foreign keys.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Only rows satisfying a predicate (e.g., WHERE active = true), reducing size and maintenance cost.

choices.label: C

choices.label: D

hard.explanation: Partial indexes target hot subsets: smaller, cheaper, faster for matching queries.

Queries must imply the predicate (WHERE status='open') to use it. Invalid rows should not exist; temp-only or blob-always readings confuse row-filtering with column choice. Size shrinks with subset selectivity.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Invalid rows should not exist if constraints enforce integrity.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Partial means row filter, not all columns by default.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Partial indexes apply to user tables with predicates.

hard.prompt: When is a partial index on Orders WHERE status = 'open' unusable for a query?

choices.label: A
choices.body: When open orders are a tiny fraction of the table.

choices.label: B
choices.body: When the query's predicate does not imply status = 'open' (e.g., it scans all statuses).

choices.label: C
choices.body: When the index is smaller than a full index.

choices.label: D
choices.body: When the query filters exactly status = 'open'.

hard.hint: Next step: check implication — query must logically stay inside the indexed subset.
hard.explanation: The planner uses partial indexes only when the query guarantees the subset.
hard.deepDive: Worked example: WHERE status='open' AND amount>100 matches the predicate → index eligible; WHERE amount>100 alone might need closed rows the index lacks → ineligible. Tiny subsets and small size are advantages, not blockers. Implication between query and index predicates is the gate: no guarantee, no use.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Small hot subsets are the ideal partial-index case.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Small size is the benefit, not a disqualifier.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Matching predicates are exactly the usable case.

hard.prompt: Histogram statistics in the catalog help the optimizer…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Estimate predicate selectivity and data distribution per column.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Encrypt data at rest with AES-256 automatically.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Store undo logs for every SELECT query.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Guarantee zero deadlocks globally.

hard.hint: Next step: after bulk changes run ANALYZE — stale stats mislead every cost.
hard.explanation: Histograms capture non-uniform distributions better than averages alone.
hard.deepDive: Worked example: salary histogram shows 80% of staff in 50–70k: salary=60k estimates 800k rows (scan), while salary=500k estimates 3 rows (index). Without histograms the uniform guess misprices both. ANALYZE refreshes them after bulk loads; skew without stats is the classic 'right index, wrong plan' cause. Security, deadlocks, and undo are untouched.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Encryption is security configuration.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: SELECT does not generate undo; DML does.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Deadlocks can still occur with accurate stats.

hard.prompt: Index merge (intersection/union) plans combine…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Two unrelated databases on different hosts without federation.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Only full-table scans because indexes cannot be combined.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Multiple single-column indexes to satisfy AND/OR predicates when one composite index is unavailable.

choices.label: D
choices.body: User passwords with hash join build sides.

hard.hint: Next step: map each AND/OR branch to an index — one index per branch enables the merge.
hard.explanation: Bitmap row sets from several indexes intersect/unite before heap access.
hard.deepDive: Worked example: WHERE city='Lyon' AND age>30 intersects the city bitmap with the age bitmap, fetching only rows in both — no (city,age) composite needed. Cross-host combination needs federation; scans are the alternative, not the ingredient. Composite indexes usually beat merges, but merges rescue queries where none exists.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Index merge is an intra-database plan choice.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Index merge exists precisely to combine indexes.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Security data is unrelated to index intersection plans.

hard.prompt: What does 'parameter sniffing' (plan caching with bound values) risk?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Reusing a plan optimized for one parameter value on a wildly different value where it performs badly.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Deleting cached plans on every execution.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Encrypting query parameters automatically.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Running every query without any plan.

hard.hint: Next step: test both extremes with the cached plan — divergent costs confirm sniffing issues.
hard.explanation: One cached shape, many selectivities: the first value's plan may poison the rest.
hard.deepDive: Worked example: status='rare' compiles an index seek; reused for status='common' (90% rows) it probes millions instead of scanning. Options: recompile hints, unknown-value optimization, or separate paths per class. No-plan and delete-every-time readings defeat caching's purpose; encryption is unrelated. Skewed columns plus cached plans invite this bug.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Eviction policies keep useful plans; per-execution deletion would thrash.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Parameter handling is planning, not encryption.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Caching always uses a plan; staleness is the risk.

hard.prompt: A query uses the wrong index after adding a better composite. What is the likely cause and fix?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Stale or missing statistics (or plan-cache stickiness); run ANALYZE and check plan hints/costs.

choices.label: B
choices.body: The new index is always ignored by design.

choices.label: C
choices.body: More indexes always slow planning to a halt.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Isolation levels force index choice permanently.

hard.hint: Next step: analyze the table, re-explain, and only then consider hints.
hard.explanation: Costs follow stats; refresh them before blaming the index.
hard.deepDive: Worked example: new (dept,salary) unused while old (dept) persists — pg_stat shows last_analyze predating the backfill, so the planner prices the composite on zero rows. ANALYZE flips the plan with no code change; pinned hints or cached plans may need clearing next. Engines use new indexes eagerly once priced correctly. Diagnose stats first, hints second.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: New usable indexes are preferred once costed correctly.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Dozens of indexes are fine; stats dominate choice here.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Isolation does not pick access paths.

hard.prompt: An UPDATE that does not touch indexed columns can still pay index costs. How?

choices.label: A
choices.body: UPDATEs never interact with indexes.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Indexes are rebuilt from scratch on every UPDATE.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Indexed columns are the only thing indexes ever store.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Non-key updates may relocate rows (or create new versions), forcing secondary indexes' locators to be updated.

hard.hint: Next step: check for row migration/version churn — hot-update failures multiply secondary maintenance.
hard.explanation: Row movement rewrites locators even when keys are unchanged.
hard.deepDive: Worked example: Postgres HOT updates stay heap-local only with free space; otherwise the new version gets a new TID and every secondary entry pointing at the row is rewritten despite email key unchanged. Secondaries store keys plus locators, so locator churn is maintenance. Full rebuilds happen on REINDEX, not per UPDATE. Fillfactor tuning and covering design blunt this hidden tax.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Locator updates are routine index maintenance.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Rebuilds are explicit operations, not per-row behavior.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Locators ride alongside keys in every entry.
